title: Complex numbers and spinning dots
summary: Read a complex number as a point on a map; find its magnitude, angle and conjugate; translate r·e^{jθ} at the easy angles; explain why a cosine is two opposite spinners; read amplitude and phase off one complex number X.
sourceNote: complex_sinusoids.pdf (Koo's note), the Day 4 slides, Lab 3 Q5–Q20. Rewritten in plain steps: one idea per card.

sections.heading: Why we need complex numbers at all

blocks.md: **You are on step 3 of the map:** splitting sounds into simple waves. To do that math cleanly, we need a way to write the spinning dot from Chapter 0 as **one** number.
blocks.label: why

blocks.md: The dot on the circle has two positions at once: how far **right** (that's cos) and how far **up** (that's sin). Normally that's two numbers. A **complex number** is just a way to pack two numbers into one, like writing a map location as one thing instead of 'x = 3, y = 4'.
That's the only reason complex numbers are in this course. Don't worry about 'the square root of −1'. For us, **j just means 'up'**.

sections.heading: A complex number is a point on a map

blocks.body: Written **a + j·b**. Go **a** to the right and **b** up. Example: 3 + 4j is the point 3 right, 4 up.

The **real part** is the number without j (right/left). The **imaginary part** is the number with j (up/down). In 3 + 4j: real part 3, imaginary part 4. 'Imaginary' is just an old name; nothing is imaginary about it.

blocks.caption: z = x + jy is an arrow from the origin. Its length is |z| = r, its angle is ∠z = θ. The conjugate z̄ is the mirror image below the real axis. Hover any part.

blocks.body: How far the point is from the center. Use Pythagoras: **|a + jb| = √(a² + b²)**. It's like the 'amplitude' of the point.
Which direction the point is in, measured counterclockwise from 'straight right'. Easy ones: straight right = 0, straight up = π/2 (90°), straight left = π (180°), straight down = −π/2 (−90°).
Flip the sign of the j part: the conjugate of 3 + 4j is 3 − 4j. It's the mirror image below the horizontal line: same distance, opposite angle.

frames.caption: Lab 3 Q5–Q8. One complex number. Read it as directions on a map.
The number without j says how far right. The number with j says how far up. So z is the point (0.5, 0.87).
Magnitude = distance from the center, by Pythagoras. It's exactly 1, so this point sits on the circle of radius 1.
Angle = which direction the point is, measured counterclockwise from 'straight right'. (Q7: magnitude 1. Q8: angle 60°.)
The conjugate flips the up/down part. It's the mirror image below the horizontal line: same distance, opposite angle.

blocks.prompt: What are the magnitude and conjugate of 6 − 8j?
What angle does the number 2j have?

blocks.md: **A shortcut worth knowing:** z times its conjugate is the magnitude squared. (3 + 4j)(3 − 4j) = 9 + 16 = 25 = 5².

sections.heading: The e^{jθ} notation: 'the point at angle θ'

blocks.body: A short way to write **the point on the circle of radius 1 at angle θ**. That's all it means in this course. (The official name is Euler's formula: e^{jθ} = cos θ + j·sin θ, meaning 'right by cos θ, up by sin θ'.)
The point at distance **r** from the center, in direction **θ**. Example: 3·e^{jπ/2} = 3 steps straight up = 3j.

blocks.title: Converting both ways

sections.heading: Spinning dots, and why a cosine is two of them

blocks.body: The dot from Chapter 0, written as one complex number that moves: **e^{j·2π·F·t}** is a dot going around the circle F times per second.

blocks.title: From one spinning dot to a cosine

lines: e^{jθ}: the dot at angle θ
frames.caption: Put the dot on the unit circle at angle θ.

lines: the dot goes around F times per second, counterclockwise
frames.caption: Let the angle grow with time (exactly like Chapter 0). Now it's a spinning dot: a complex sinusoid.
Put a minus sign in front: it spins the other way. People call that a 'negative frequency'. It just means clockwise.
Add the two dots together. Their up-down parts are always opposite, so they cancel. Their left-right parts are always equal, so they double.
Divide by 2: a normal cosine wave is the average of two dots spinning opposite ways. That's why a spectrum shows a cosine as TWO lines, at +F and −F, each half as tall.

blocks.prompt: What do you get if you add e^{j2π·5·t} and e^{−j2π·5·t}?
blocks.answer: 2·cos(2π·5·t): a real cosine at 5 Hz with amplitude 2. The up-down parts cancel.

blocks.body: Thinking a 'negative frequency' is something weird. It only means the dot spins clockwise. Every real sound shows up at both +F and −F in a two-sided spectrum.

sections.heading: One number that holds amplitude AND phase

blocks.md: Remember the three dials from Chapter 0: A (how tall), F (how fast), ϕ (where it starts). Here's the neat trick: **A and ϕ can be packed into one complex number**.

blocks.body: **X = A · e^{jϕ}**: the point at distance A in direction ϕ. Its **magnitude** is the amplitude. Its **angle** is the phase. So one complex number tells you both how tall a wave is and where it starts.

blocks.title: Reading A and ϕ out of X
blocks.body:
X = 4·e^{jπ/2}      →  A = 4,   ϕ = π/2
X = 2j              →  distance 2, pointing up  →  A = 2, ϕ = π/2
X = 0.354 − 0.354j  →  |X| = √(0.125 + 0.125) = 0.5
                        angle: right and down equally → −π/4

blocks.md: **Why this matters for every later lab:** a spectrum gives you one complex number X for each frequency. **|X| = how much of that frequency** (that's the magnitude spectrum). **The angle of X = its phase** (the phase spectrum).

blocks.body: In a two-sided spectrum a cosine of amplitude A appears as two lines of height **A/2** (at +F and −F). To get the real amplitude back, double it: A = 2·|X|.

blocks.prompt: A spectrum says X = 3j at some frequency (two-sided). What are the cosine's amplitude and phase?
blocks.answer: |X| = 3, so A = 2 × 3 = 6. The angle of 3j is π/2, so ϕ = π/2.

exercises.title: One point, three ways
exercises.prompt: z = −3 + 3j. Find |z|, its angle, write it as r·e^{jθ}, and write its conjugate.
hints: Plot it: 3 left, 3 up.
Distance: √(9 + 9). Direction: halfway between straight up (π/2) and straight left (π).
Conjugate: flip the sign of the j part.
exercises.why: Every coefficient numpy gives you in a Fourier lab is a complex number like this; reading it is half the lab.

exercises.title: Why a cosine is two spinners
exercises.prompt: Explain in two sentences why e^{j2πFt} + e^{−j2πFt} is a real cosine, then say what that means for the spectrum of a 100 Hz cosine.
hints: One dot spins counterclockwise, the other clockwise, at the same speed.
What happens to their up-down positions? Their left-right positions?
So how many lines does the spectrum show, and where?
solution: The up-down parts are always opposite and cancel; the left-right parts are always equal and add up to 2·cos(2πFt).
So a 100 Hz cosine shows up in a two-sided spectrum as two lines, at +100 Hz and −100 Hz, each half the cosine's amplitude.
exercises.why: This is the reason every FFT output has a mirror image, and why you double |X| to get the real amplitude.

exercises.title: Easy point
exercises.prompt: What is e^{jπ} as a plain number?
hints: Read each option out loud and cross off the ones that are clearly wrong.
The chapter's cards in this section have the exact fact you need.
Pick the one that matches the definition word for word.
solution: e^{jπ} is the point at angle π (180°) on the unit circle: straight left, which is −1.
exercises.why: The four easy points come up in almost every coefficient calculation.

choices.feedback: Right: angle π is half a lap, straight left.

exercises.title: Direction
exercises.prompt: What is the angle of the complex number −4j?
hints: Read each option out loud and cross off the ones that are clearly wrong.
The chapter's cards in this section have the exact fact you need.
Pick the one that matches the definition word for word.
solution: −4j has no real part and a negative j part: straight down, angle −π/2.
exercises.why: Phase spectra are made of exactly these angles.

exercises.title: Two spinners
hints: Read each option out loud and cross off the ones that are clearly wrong.
The chapter's cards in this section have the exact fact you need.
Pick the one that matches the definition word for word.
solution: The two dots spin opposite ways at 10 Hz. Up-down: +sin and −sin cancel. Left-right: cos + cos = 2·cos.
exercises.why: This is why every real signal's FFT is mirror-symmetric.

exercises.title: Fill in: amplitude from X
exercises.prompt: A two-sided spectrum shows X = 1.5 at 100 Hz. The cosine's amplitude A is ____.
hints: Two-sided: each side holds half the amplitude.
